questions.q: A client having an acute asthma attack has been wheezing loudly. Which change would suggest the attack is becoming life-threatening?
options: The client is able to speak in full sentences
The client starts coughing up clear sputum
The wheeze disappears and the chest becomes quiet
The wheeze becomes louder on breathing out
questions.explanation: A silent chest means very little air is moving in and out of the lungs. It is an ominous sign, not an improvement. Call for urgent help, give oxygen and the prescribed bronchodilator, and prepare for senior review.

questions.q: A client has a chest drain connected to an underwater seal. Which action is correct?
options: Clamp the drain whenever the client walks
Raise the bottle above the chest to help drainage
Strip the tubing every hour to keep it clear
Keep the drainage bottle below the level of the client's chest at all times
questions.explanation: Keeping the bottle below chest level stops fluid and air from flowing back into the pleural space. Do not clamp a drain that is still draining air, because this can cause a tension pneumothorax. Stripping the tubing is not routine practice.

questions.q: A client is prescribed a bronchodilator inhaler and a corticosteroid inhaler. Which instruction is correct?
options: Use the corticosteroid first, then the bronchodilator straight away
Use the bronchodilator first, wait a few minutes, then use the corticosteroid inhaler
The order makes no difference to how well they work
Use both inhalers together in one breath
questions.explanation: The bronchodilator opens the airways so the corticosteroid can reach deeper into the lungs. Ask the client to rinse the mouth after the steroid inhaler to help prevent oral thrush.

questions.q: Which finding would the nurse expect in a client with left-sided heart failure?
options: Warm dry skin and a slow pulse
Distended neck veins and ascites
Crackles in the lungs and breathlessness when lying flat
Swollen ankles and an enlarged liver
questions.explanation: Left-sided failure causes blood to back up into the lungs, giving breathlessness, orthopnoea, cough and crackles. Peripheral oedema, an enlarged liver, ascites and distended neck veins are features of right-sided failure.

questions.q: A client with hypertension is started on hydrochlorothiazide. Which advice is most appropriate?
options: Stop the tablet once the blood pressure returns to normal
Take the tablet in the morning and eat potassium-rich foods such as bananas unless told otherwise
Take the tablet at bedtime so it works overnight
Restrict all fluids to 500 mL a day
questions.explanation: Taking a diuretic in the morning avoids waking at night to pass urine. Thiazides cause potassium loss, so potassium-rich foods and blood tests are usually advised. Blood pressure medicines should not be stopped without advice, because the pressure will rise again.

questions.q: A client returns to the ward after cardiac catheterisation through the femoral artery. Which finding needs immediate action?
options: Mild tenderness at the puncture site
The client is lying flat with the leg kept straight
A growing swelling at the groin site with increasing pain
Pedal pulses present and equal in both feet
questions.explanation: A growing swelling suggests bleeding into the tissues (an expanding haematoma). Apply firm pressure over the site and call the doctor urgently. Present, equal pedal pulses and lying flat with the leg straight are expected.

questions.q: A client with diabetes is found sweating, shaky and confused. The blood glucose is 2.8 mmol/L and the client can swallow. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give the next dose of insulin
Recheck the blood glucose after one hour
Give a high-protein snack only
Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as a glass of juice or glucose
questions.explanation: Treat hypoglycaemia immediately with fast-acting sugar, then recheck the glucose in about 15 minutes and follow with a longer-acting snack once the client has recovered. If the client cannot swallow, they need intravenous glucose or glucagon.

questions.q: Which finding is characteristic of diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: A blood glucose below 3 mmol/L
Deep, rapid breathing with a fruity smell on the breath
Slow, shallow breathing with pale skin
Cool, clammy skin and tremors
questions.explanation: In ketoacidosis the body blows off carbon dioxide through deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, and ketones give the breath a fruity smell. Blood glucose is high. Cool, clammy skin and tremors point to hypoglycaemia.

questions.q: Which set of findings is expected in a client with hyperthyroidism?
options: Weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation
A slow pulse and dry, coarse skin
Weight loss despite a good appetite, heat intolerance and palpitations
Fatigue, a puffy face and a hoarse voice
questions.explanation: Excess thyroid hormone speeds up the metabolism, causing weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, palpitations and anxiety. The other options describe an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism).

questions.q: A client with advanced chronic kidney disease has a raised serum potassium. Which dietary advice is appropriate?
options: Use a salt substitute instead of table salt
Drink as much fluid as possible to flush the kidneys
Eat more oranges and bananas for extra vitamins
Limit high-potassium foods such as bananas, oranges and potatoes
questions.explanation: Failing kidneys cannot remove potassium, so high-potassium foods are limited. Many salt substitutes contain potassium chloride and should be avoided. Fluid is usually restricted according to urine output and swelling.

questions.q: Which finding would the nurse expect in a child with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Burning on passing urine with a foul smell
Dark tea- or cola-coloured urine with puffiness around the eyes
Large volumes of pale, dilute urine
Low blood pressure with dry skin
questions.explanation: Inflamed glomeruli leak blood and protein, causing haematuria, oedema (often around the eyes first), reduced urine output and raised blood pressure. Burning and foul-smelling urine suggest a urinary tract infection.

questions.q: A client with a peptic ulcer suddenly develops severe abdominal pain and a rigid, board-like abdomen. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
options: Constipation
Gastritis
Pyloric stenosis
Perforation of the ulcer
questions.explanation: A sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen means stomach contents are leaking into the peritoneal cavity. This is a surgical emergency: keep the client nil by mouth, and call the doctor urgently.

questions.q: A client with liver cirrhosis has ascites. Which nursing measure is most appropriate?
options: Encourage a high-sodium diet
Encourage the client to drink at least 3 litres of fluid a day
Measure the abdominal girth and weigh the client daily
Give ibuprofen for abdominal discomfort
questions.explanation: Daily weight and girth measurements show whether fluid is building up or clearing. Sodium is restricted, fluids may be limited, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are avoided in cirrhosis because they raise the risk of bleeding and kidney injury.

questions.q: Which position is best for a client with raised intracranial pressure?
options: Lying flat with a pillow under the head
Head turned to one side with the hips bent
Head of the bed raised about 30 degrees, with the head in a neutral midline position
Trendelenburg position
questions.explanation: Raising the head about 30 degrees and keeping the neck straight helps venous blood drain from the head. Avoid neck flexion, hip flexion and head-down positions, which raise the pressure.

questions.q: Which is the earliest sign of increasing intracranial pressure?
options: A slow pulse with a widened pulse pressure
An irregular breathing pattern
A fixed, dilated pupil
A change in level of consciousness, such as restlessness or drowsiness
questions.explanation: The brain is very sensitive to rising pressure, so a change in level of consciousness comes first. A slow pulse with a high systolic pressure, fixed pupils and irregular breathing are late signs.

questions.q: A client who has had a stroke is drowsy and has a weak cough. What should the nurse do before offering any food or drink?
options: Assess the swallow and keep the client nil by mouth until it has been checked
Offer thin fluids first to test the swallow
Ask the relatives to feed the client
Lay the client flat during meals
questions.explanation: Stroke often weakens the swallow, and feeding before it is assessed risks aspiration pneumonia. Keep nil by mouth until a swallow screen is done, and feed only when the client is sitting upright.

questions.q: A client with a fractured femur develops sudden breathlessness, confusion and a small red-purple rash over the chest. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
options: Fat embolism
Deep infection of the skin
Constipation
Muscle spasm
questions.explanation: Fat embolism can follow fractures of long bones, usually within one to three days. It causes breathlessness, confusion and petechiae. Call for urgent help and give oxygen.

questions.q: Which finding suggests compartment syndrome in a limb with a plaster cast?
options: Mild itching under the cast
Severe pain that is not relieved by analgesia and worsens when the toes are moved
Pain that is relieved by raising the limb
Warm pink toes that refill quickly after pressing
questions.explanation: Rising pressure inside the limb causes pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch, numbness or tingling, and later pallor and loss of pulses. It is an emergency: report at once.

questions.q: A client returns from theatre still unconscious after a general anaesthetic. What is the nurse's first priority?
options: Complete the intake and output chart
Maintain a clear airway and position the client to prevent aspiration
Check the wound dressing before anything else
Offer sips of water
questions.explanation: Airway comes first. An unconscious client can obstruct the airway or inhale vomit, so position the client on the side (or as ordered), support the airway and monitor breathing before other tasks.

questions.q: Before a client goes to theatre for elective surgery, which finding should the nurse report?
options: The client has removed dentures and jewellery
The client has fasted for eight hours
The signed consent form is in the notes
The client had breakfast two hours ago
questions.explanation: A full stomach raises the risk of vomiting and aspiration under anaesthesia. Report it to the anaesthetist and surgeon, because the operation may need to be delayed.

questions.q: A client with vomiting and diarrhoea is becoming hypovolaemic. Which is an early sign?
options: A rapid pulse
Increased urine output
A slow, bounding pulse
A rise in blood pressure
questions.explanation: The body first compensates for fluid loss by speeding up the heart. Falling blood pressure, low urine output and confusion appear as the loss continues.

questions.q: Using the Parkland formula (4 mL x body weight in kg x % total body surface area burned), how much fluid does a 70 kg adult with 20% burns need in the first 24 hours?
questions.explanation: 4 x 70 x 20 = 5,600 mL. Half of this (2,800 mL) is given in the first 8 hours counted from the time of the burn, and the rest over the next 16 hours. The formula is a guide and is adjusted to the client's urine output.

questions.q: What is the correct immediate first aid for a thermal burn?
options: Apply butter or cooking oil
Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes
Burst any blisters to let the fluid out
Apply ice directly to the burn
questions.explanation: Cool running water stops the burning process and reduces pain and tissue damage. Ice can cause further injury, greasy substances trap heat and raise the risk of infection, and blisters should be left intact.
